title: Chapter Two
collection: The Life of St Andrew the Fool

pairs.en: *Feigning madness, he is bound.* *He is enlightened by revelations.* *He is attacked by demons and set free, and he is called to God's service.*

**7.** When the blessed man heard those words he woke out of that deepest sleep, still marvelling at the fragrance that had come over him — a scent on his face that was awesome, invisible, past understanding.

Early in the morning he came to me, unworthy as I am, and told me plainly what had happened. I was astonished to hear of his ecstasy, and more astonished still to see his face giving off light, and a divine fragrance, awesome and beyond comparison.

So the two of us weighed the matter together, and we judged that he should take on the appearance of a man possessed by a demon and out of his mind — because of the One who had said to him, *Become a fool for my sake, and on the day of my kingdom you will sit as master of many good things.* There was no other way for him to get free of the master who owned his body. It is hard for any man to release his own household slave while he lives — and hardest of all when it is for the work of God, with the devil obstructing it out of envy.

**8.** The next night, at midnight, he got up and prayed; and when he had finished his prayer he took a knife and went out to the well beside his master's bedroom. There he stripped off the clothes he was wearing and began cutting them into small pieces with the knife, and like a man moon-struck he began muttering confused words, in the way the moon-struck do.

His master woke and heard the muttering, and could not think what it might be, least of all at that hour. He supposed it must be some evil spirit belonging to the well, out at that hour to trick whoever came looking for water. So he lay still until morning.

At daybreak his cook went out to fill up with water, saw what had become of Andrew, and was appalled. He left his water-jar where it stood and went to tell his master, who was still chanting the morning psalms. His master was astounded to hear it — that Andrew had lost his wits and was sitting at the mouth of the well. He went down at once to see him, and the whole household gathered round.

Most of them wept over him, believing he had truly been driven mad by demons. His master was deeply grieved at what had happened and could do nothing at all to help him; so he had him carried to the holy church of the martyr Anastasia — the one at ta Machellou, by the meat market — and gave orders that he be bound in the saint's chain, paying money to the church warden so that he would be looked after all the better.

**9.** All day long the blessed man kept up his counterfeit words, as though he really were out of his mind. But at night he wept and prayed, begging the Martyr of Christ to appear to him and tell him plainly whether what he had begun was pleasing to God.

When he had rested a little from his weeping and his prayer — behold, visibly, five women stood there, and before them walked an old man of great glory, on beautiful feet. They went round the sick who were kept there, visiting them one by one; and when they had passed the rest, they came to him too, the old man first and the holy women after him.

Then the old man looked at him steadily, and smiled at him kindly, turning over some good thought about him. And he said to the most radiant of the women, as though gently teasing her: *Lady Anastasia, are you never going to heal this one?*

She said: *My lord and master, another has already claimed him, and he needs nobody now.* *The one who said to him, “Become a fool for my sake, and you will sit as master of many good things in my kingdom” — that one has healed him, and he has no more need of a physician.* *He knows the trade he has learned.* *He will not let go of it until his last breath; he will become for our God a chosen vessel, holy, and beloved in the Spirit.*
The old man said: *I knew that too, my lady.* *I said it out of a certain restraint.*

**10.** When they had said this to one another, with Andrew watching, they gave him their peace and went into the inner part of the church to pray. And from then until dawn came and the warden struck the wooden board, he did not see a single one of them go out or come in again.

Andrew marvelled, and praised God in his spirit, and thanked the great martyr Anastasia for coming so quickly to his prayers. He sat all that day in his chains, tasting no food, saying nothing but his counterfeit words.

Then when night fell as usual and he was keeping vigil, and towards midnight was secretly making his customary prayers and entreaties in the hidden chamber of his heart, offering them to God and to the martyr — suddenly the devil came at him with a crowd of demons, holding an axe in his hand. Some of the demons had knives, some clubs, others swords and spears, and others ropes — for that dragon was a commander of a thousand, and that is why so many of them had come with him to destroy the blessed man. He gnashed his teeth from a distance, for he had taken the shape of an old Ethiopian, and rushed at the saint to strike him with the axe he was holding, and every demon with him.
**11.** But the blessed young man stretched out his hands to the Lord with many tears, and said only this: *Holy John the Theologian, help me.*

At once there was thunder out of the height, and a sound like a great crowd; and behold, a huge old man, wide-eyed, a little bald, his face brighter than the sun, with a great multitude behind him. And he said to those with him, in anger: *Secure the gates.* *Not one of them is to escape our hands.* There were many of them, and they did it in a moment.
When every one of the demons had been caught, one Moor whispered to his companion: *We are in for it.* *John is harsh, and he punishes us terribly.*

Then that venerable old man gave the order, and they took the chain off blessed Andrew's neck; and he took it, walked over to the outer gate, stood there and said to his companions: *Bring them to me one at a time.*

They brought the first. He said, *Stretch him out on the ground* — and taking the blessed man's chain in his own hands he folded it in three and gave him something like a hundred lashes. And the demon cried out exactly like a man: *Have mercy, have mercy, have mercy.* After that he had a second stretched out, and he got the same.

Hearing that *Have mercy*, blessed Andrew could not help himself and was seized with laughter — it seemed so absurd that Ethiopians should be pinned down like men and beaten, and feel it. But in truth it was God who was inflicting those blows: their own nature, having no body, could not really have been hurt at all.

So they stretched out the third as well, and he suffered the same; and while they were laying into them vigorously, the others called out to the ones who had been beaten and let go, saying to each: *Off you go, and teach all this to your father Satan — if it pleases him.*

**12.** When they had all withdrawn, the men in white vanished from that place; but the handsome old man came to the blessed man, put the chain back on him, and said kindly: *Do you see how quickly I hurried to help you?* *I want you to know that I care very much about you.* *The Master has appointed me and charged me to watch over whatever is truly good for you and best for your salvation, and to be your umpire.* *So hold out, and be tested in everything.* *It will not be long before you too are released — at your own Lord's own will — to go wherever seems good in your eyes.*
Andrew said: *My lord, who are you?* *I do not know you.*
And he said: *I am the one who leaned on the undefiled and life-giving breast of our Lord Jesus Christ.*
And with that, turning as it were into a flash of lightning, he was gone from his sight.

Blessed Andrew marvelled at the unspeakable goodness of God and glorified him greatly — that he had become his helper in every word and deed, and had delivered him so swiftly from the dark spirits that rose against him. And he said in secret: *Lord Jesus Christ, great and beyond words is your power.* *Your inward mercies are glorified beyond nature, in that you pity me, who am nothing, and take care of me;* *I count that strange, and a great wonder.* *Keep me then, Lord, more and more in your truth, and let me find favour before you, Most High, Almighty, Awesome and Past Understanding.*

**13.** While he was praying like this, night came on; and when he had slept a little, he saw in a vision that he was in a royal palace, and the king of that palace called him. As he stood beside him, the king said: *Do you want to serve me with your whole soul?* *I will make you one of the great men of my palace.*
Andrew said: *And who would refuse what is good?* *It is the very thing I want.*
The king said: *Well then, if you want it, take a taste of what my service is.*

And with the word he gave him something like snow. He took it and put it in his mouth, and it was sweet in a way the mind of man cannot compare with anything. It was only a little, and when he had eaten it he thought its sweetness was turning into a divine myrrh.

Then the king gave him another small thing, like a little ball of snow, and said to him, *Take this and eat it too.* He took it and ate — and it was sharp, and bitter beyond wormwood, and all the more shocking for coming straight after that other sweetness and delight.

Seeing him staggered by it, the king said: *You see how you cannot bear the bitterness of the taste?* *By these two things I have let you feel what my service really is.* *For this is the narrow and hard-pressed road, and it is the one that leads to life.*
**14.** The blessed man said: *This is a bitter business, Master.* *Who could eat such things and serve you?*
The king said: *You have noticed the bitter — did you not notice the sweet?* *Did I not give you the sweet first, and the bitter after?*
He said: *Yes, master.* *But it is in the bitter alone that you have set out for your servant the picture of the hard-pressed road.*

The king said: *No.* *The road runs between the two, through the sweet and through the bitter.* *In the bitter you have been shown the feel of the contests and the labours undergone for my sake; in the pleasant and the sweet, the dew and the refreshing of my goodness that comes to those who are tested for my sake.* *So it is not all bitterness, and not all sweetness, but now the one and now the other, each following the other.* *If you agree, then settle it with me, and let me know.*
Andrew said: *Give me the same things again.* *I will look, and then I will tell you.*

So he gave him the bitter again, and then the sweet. And being shaken more than before by the bitter taste, he said: *I cannot serve you if this is what I must eat.* *The business is bitter, and it is heavy.*

At that the king smiled, and drew out of his breast something else of a different kind — fiery to look at, by nature exceedingly fragrant, the colour of flowers — and said: *Take this and eat, and you will forget everything you have seen and heard.*
He took it and ate; and for hours afterwards he was not himself for the delight and the boundless joy of it, but was as though plunged into some vast fragrance and glory and gladness.

When he came to himself he fell at the feet of that great king and begged him: *Have mercy on me, my good master, and do not throw me out of your service from this day on.* *For now I truly know how very sweet the road of your service is, and I will never bow my neck to anyone but you.*

And the king said: *If this bright taste amazed you — believe me when I tell you that of all the good things I have, this is the cheapest of them.* *But if you will stay with me, everything of mine is yours, and I will make you co-heir of my kingdom.*
Having said this to him, the king let him go. And blessed Andrew woke from sleep and kept all of it in his heart, and wondered what it might mean.

**15.** He stayed in the martyr's church about four months. When the wardens saw he was not getting better but worse, they told his master how things stood. Theognostos heard it, wrote him off as plainly and truly demon-possessed, and ordered that he be released from his bonds at once and let go wherever he wanted.
From that day he ran about the broad streets of the city, playing the part of that marvellous Symeon of old.

And when evening came he came to me, unworthy as I am, while I was sleeping alone indoors; and smiling, he began to wet his honoured face with tears. We held each other a long while, and kissed each other, and went to sleep.

I kept asking him about himself — how, after so many days in chains, he had been let go; and he told me everything, with all gentleness and mildness. For to me alone, my brothers and most faithful friends, he spoke soundly and without pretence. To everyone else he was a man deranged, or he did not speak at all.
